title: Design a URL Shortener
summary: Build short links that are hard to guess, redirect within 100 ms at peak, stop working when disabled, and collect analytics without slowing anyone down.
body:
## Practice first

Design a service that turns a long URL into a short link (for example `sho.rt/aZ3k9Qx`) and redirects anyone who visits the short link to the original destination. Owners can pick a custom alias, set an expiry and disable a link later.

Try a 10-minute sketch on paper before reading on. List the requirements and entities, write the two main endpoints, draw a working baseline, and choose two deep dives. Then compare your decisions with this walkthrough. You do not need the same product names or the same design; you need reasoning you can defend.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Create a short link** for a long URL, optionally with a custom alias and an expiry time.
2. **Be redirected** from the short link to the destination when they visit it.
3. **Disable or delete** a link they own, after which visits stop redirecting.

Out of scope for this session: a full analytics dashboard (we only emit click events), link editing UI, QR codes, team workspaces and billing. Authentication exists but is not designed here; ownership is derived from the authenticated caller.

Keep two product rules in view. People paste private document links into shorteners, so generated aliases must not let someone count their way through the links. But an alias is still public: knowing it never grants permission to view private content.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** about 100 million new links per month; redirects outnumber creations roughly 100 to 1.
- **Redirect latency:** p99 under 100 ms measured at the edge of the serving region, excluding the visitor's last-mile network.
- **Availability vs consistency, per operation:** redirects favour availability (99.99%); a slightly stale answer for a few seconds is acceptable *except* after a disable, which must take effect within a bounded window (say 60 seconds). Creation favours consistency: two users must never receive the same alias.
- **Durability:** a created link must never be lost or silently rebound to a different destination for its lifetime.
- **Analytics:** click events are eventually consistent and must never sit on the redirect's critical path.

## Back-of-the-envelope

Only the numbers that change a decision:

- **Write rate:** 100M / (30 × 86,400 s) ≈ 39 creates/s average; with a 10× peak, about 400/s. A single well-provisioned relational primary handles this comfortably, so we do **not** need sharding or a distributed ID service on day one.
- **Read rate:** 100 × 39 ≈ 3,900 redirects/s average, perhaps 40,000/s at peak. That is too much to send every request to one primary but trivial for an in-memory cache, so a **cache in front of the database is justified**.
- **Storage:** say 500 bytes per row (destination up to ~2 KB is rare; most are short) × 1.2B links/year ≈ 600 GB/year. Five years is about 3 TB including indexes: fits a single large Postgres instance or a small sharded cluster later.
- **Alias space:** seven Base62 characters give 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion values. After five years (6B links) the space is about 0.17% full, so a random alias collides on insert with probability about 0.0017: rare, but not zero. We still need a **uniqueness check that is atomic**.
- **Hot set:** link popularity is heavily skewed. If 20% of links take 80% of clicks and the cache holds the hottest ~10M rows at ~500 B each, that is about 5 GB of memory: one cache node, replicated for availability.

## Core entities

- **Link:** alias, destination URL, owner, created/expiry/disabled timestamps.
- **User:** the owner identity from the auth system.
- **ClickEvent:** alias, timestamp, coarse client metadata; produced asynchronously.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USER ||--o{ LINK : owns
    LINK ||--o{ CLICK_EVENT : records
    LINK {
        string alias PK
        string destination
        string owner_id
        datetime expires_at
        datetime disabled_at
    }
    CLICK_EVENT {
        string event_id PK
        string alias
        datetime clicked_at
    }
```

`alias` is the primary key, which gives us the unique index that decides collisions. Click events live in a separate analytics store, not in the transactional database.

## API

```http
POST /v1/links
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c...
{ "destination": "https://example.com/very/long/path", "customAlias": "spring-sale", "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }

201 Created
{ "alias": "spring-sale", "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/spring-sale", "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
409 Conflict   (custom alias already taken)
```

```http
GET /{alias}
302 Found
Location: https://example.com/very/long/path
Cache-Control: private, max-age=60

404 Not Found  (unknown, expired or disabled; same body for all three)
```

```http
DELETE /v1/links/{alias}
Authorization: Bearer <token>
204 No Content
```

Owner is taken from the token, never from the body. Replaying the same `Idempotency-Key` with the same payload returns the original link; reusing the key with a different payload returns 422. Listing a user's links (`GET /v1/links?cursor=...`) uses cursor pagination on `(owner_id, created_at)`.

## High-level design

**Requirement 1, create.** A stateless Link API validates the destination (allowed schemes `http`/`https`, length limits, optional malware check), generates an alias and inserts the row. The database's unique constraint is the only authority on availability: we never do "SELECT then INSERT", because two concurrent requests can both see the alias as free.

**Requirement 2, redirect.** A separate Redirect service (it has a very different load profile) looks up the alias, checks `expires_at` and `disabled_at`, and returns a 302. It reads through a cache first.

**Requirement 3, disable.** The Link API sets `disabled_at` and deletes the cache entry. The cache entry also has a short TTL, so even if the delete is lost the disable takes effect within the TTL.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Creator client"] --> GW["API gateway (auth, rate limit)"]
    V["Visitor browser"] --> R["Redirect service"]
    GW --> API["Link API"]
    API --> DB[("Postgres primary")]
    DB --> REP[("Read replicas")]
    API -.->|"invalidate"| CACHE[("Redis cache")]
    R --> CACHE
    R -->|"miss"| REP
    R --> Q[["Click event stream"]]
    Q --> AN[("Analytics store")]
```

Follow a visit to `aZ3k9Qx`. The browser reaches the Redirect service, which checks Redis. A hit needs only an expiry and disabled-flag check before a 302, usually in a few milliseconds. A miss reads a replica and fills the cache with a TTL. The service then emits a click event without waiting for the stream; a stream outage must not break the redirect. Creating a link takes a different path: gateway authentication and per-user rate limits, then the Link API and primary database.

## Deep dives

### 1. Generating unique, non-guessable aliases (consistency on create)

**Bad: hash the destination.** Taking the first seven characters of MD5(destination) makes the same URL from two users collide by design, and truncated hashes of different URLs still collide. You need a collision path anyway.

**Good: global counter encoded in Base62.** A single sequence (or a range-allocating ID service handing out blocks of 1,000 per API node) guarantees uniqueness without retries. But the output is sequential: anyone can walk `aZ3k9Qx`, `aZ3k9Qy`… and discover private links. You could encrypt the counter with a format-preserving cipher or a keyed permutation to make it look random; that works but adds key management.

**Great for this prompt: random alias plus unique constraint.** Pick seven characters uniformly from the Base62 alphabet using a cryptographically secure random source (about 41.7 bits of entropy), `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, and retry with a new value if zero rows were inserted, up to a small bound (say 5). With the space under 1% full, the expected number of retries is negligible, and the alias is unpredictable. Custom aliases use the same insert: a conflict returns 409 instead of retrying.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant API as Link API
    participant DB as Postgres
    API->>API: alias = random Base62 (7 chars)
    API->>DB: INSERT link ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    DB-->>API: 0 rows (collision)
    API->>API: alias = new random value
    API->>DB: INSERT link ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    DB-->>API: 1 row
    API-->>API: return alias
```

Let the database settle the race. A collision returns zero rows, so the API draws another alias. If the namespace grows beyond a few percent full, make new aliases eight characters long rather than letting retries climb.

### 2. Fast redirects at peak (latency and read scale)

**Bad: every redirect reads the primary.** At 40,000 reads/s the primary spends its capacity on reads, and write latency for creators suffers.

**Good: read replicas.** Replicas scale reads horizontally, but replication lag means a link created a moment ago may 404 on its first click, which is exactly when a creator tests it.

**Great: cache-aside in Redis with replicas behind it, plus read-your-writes handling.** The cache absorbs the skewed hot set (≈5 GB). On a cache miss for an alias created in the last few seconds, fall back to the primary if the replica returns nothing; alternatively, write-through the new link into the cache at creation time so the first click hits. Protect against stampedes on hot keys with request coalescing (one in-flight load per alias per node), and cache negative results ("not found") briefly so random-alias scanners do not hammer the database.

Should the redirect be cached by browsers and CDNs? A 301 is cached aggressively and indefinitely by many browsers, which would make disablement and click counting impossible. Use 302 (or 307) with `Cache-Control: private, max-age=60`, matching the disable SLA. If the product truly wants permanent, immutable links, 301 with a long max-age is a legitimate trade-off that you should state explicitly.

### 3. Making disable take effect (bounded staleness)

The disable path has three caches: Redis, any CDN in front of the Redirect service, and browsers. Deleting the Redis key is necessary but not sufficient, because the delete can fail or race with a concurrent cache fill that read the old row from a lagging replica.

**Bad:** rely on invalidation alone; a lost message leaves a disabled phishing link live forever.

**Good:** invalidate and set a short TTL (60 s) so the worst case is bounded.

**Great:** invalidate, TTL, and store a `version` in each cache entry; fills only overwrite if their version is newer, and disables bump the version. For abuse takedowns, also purge the CDN path explicitly. Expiry needs no invalidation at all because the redirect service checks `expires_at` on every request, including cache hits.

### 4. Analytics without hurting redirects (availability)

Click counting must not add latency or failure modes to the redirect. Emit an event to a log such as Kafka asynchronously from a local buffer. If the product only needs approximate counts, a bounded in-memory buffer that drops on overflow is fine and simple. If clicks are billable, buffer to local disk or require a durable acknowledgement before responding, accepting a few extra milliseconds, and give each event an ID so downstream consumers deduplicate at-least-once delivery. Aggregation (per-link counts per hour) runs in a stream processor into a columnar analytics store.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["Redirect service"] --> B["Local event buffer"]
    B -->|"async batch"| K[["Kafka clicks topic"]]
    K --> SP["Stream aggregator"]
    SP --> OLAP[("Columnar analytics store")]
    SP -.->|"dedupe by event_id"| SP
```

The redirect returns before the event leaves the process. The buffer absorbs short Kafka outages; the aggregator deduplicates by event ID because producers retry.

### 5. Growing past one database (durability and scale)

At ~3 TB after five years, one primary with synchronous standby and point-in-time backups is enough. If writes or storage outgrow it, shard by `hash(alias)`: every redirect already carries the alias, so lookups stay single-shard. Listing a user's links then becomes a scatter-gather, so keep a secondary index table keyed by `owner_id`. Name the trigger for sharding (for example, sustained primary CPU above 60% or storage approaching the instance limit) rather than sharding preemptively.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a working baseline with a clear create and redirect path, a correct uniqueness story (a unique constraint, not check-then-insert), a cache for reads, and sensible 302 vs 301 reasoning when prompted.
- **Senior:** drives the deep dives without prompting: enumeration risk of counters, replica lag on first click, cache invalidation for disables, async analytics with explicit loss tolerance, and numbers that justify (or reject) sharding.
- **Staff:** frames the trade-offs as product decisions (permanent links vs revocable links, approximate vs billable analytics), designs abuse controls and operational signals (collision retry rate, cache hit ratio, disable propagation time), and explains how the design evolves across regions without breaking alias uniqueness.

## Common mistakes

- Using a sequential counter and calling the aliases "random" because they are Base62.
- Checking alias availability with a SELECT before inserting.
- Returning 301 by default, then promising disables and click counts that browsers will never let you observe.
- Putting analytics writes synchronously on the redirect path.
- Sharding, adding a distributed ID service and Kafka before showing that one database cannot serve 400 writes/s.
- Treating the short URL as an access token for private content.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Each functional requirement maps to an endpoint and a component.
- [ ] Alias uniqueness is enforced atomically by the datastore.
- [ ] Generated aliases are not enumerable, and you can say why.
- [ ] Redirect status code and cache headers match the disable and analytics requirements.
- [ ] The first click after creation works despite replica lag.
- [ ] Analytics failure cannot fail a redirect, and the loss policy is stated.
- [ ] At least one estimate changed a decision (cache yes, sharding not yet).
- [ ] Destinations are validated to limit phishing and open-redirect abuse.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html)
- [MDN: HTTP redirections](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Redirections)
- [Redis documentation](https://redis.io/docs/latest/)
keyTakeaways: Let the datastore's unique constraint settle competing alias inserts. A SELECT before the insert cannot make creation safe.
Base62 changes how a counter looks, not how predictable it is. Permute sequential values or use secure random aliases to prevent enumeration.
At 40,000 skewed reads/s, a cache earns its place. At 400 writes/s, sharding is not yet needed.
Choose redirect codes and cache headers with the product team: a cached 301 gives up reliable revocation and click counting.
Make disables stick with invalidation and a bounded TTL. Send analytics asynchronously, and say which events may be lost.
